Paper_name: Self-prioritization depends on assumed task-relevance of self-association
Summary: Three experiments tested whether the self-prioritization effect (SPE) depends on participants believing that self-associations are relevant to the task. In a standard matching task, participants associated shapes with identities (self, friend, none). They then performed a pseudo-word matching task where familiar labels were replaced. When instructions led participants to believe the self-association was task-relevant (Experiments 1 and 3), the SPE was observed in the pseudo-word task. When instructions correctly indicated the association was task-irrelevant (Experiment 2), the SPE disappeared. The results show that self-prioritization can occur even without established self-stimuli, but only if the self-association is represented as relevant to the task goals.
Author: Mateusz Woźniak, Guenther Knoblich
Conclusion: The main finding is that the self-prioritization effect is not automatic but depends on cognitive control. It emerges only when participants represent the association between a stimulus and the self as being relevant to the current task. The SPE was observed with pseudo-words (lacking prior self-association) only when task instructions framed the self-link as relevant, demonstrating that assumed task-relevance is a critical moderator of the effect.
